newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan oil firms to cope easily with spill damages.
newsitem.headline: Japan oil firms to cope easily with spill damages.

text.p: Fluctuating crude oil prices and a bearish yen pose a greater threat to Japanese oil company earnings than any compensation payments that might arise out of a recent oil spill, industry analysts say.
A Russian-owned tanker carrying 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of fuel oil broke in half in stormy seas in the Sea of Japan on January 2 causing one of Japan's worst oil spill disaster.

Although any claims for damages have yet to be calculated, they are widely expected to exceed the maximum liability that a tanker the size of the 13,157-tonne tanker Nakhodka would face under the terms of an international code -- which would be about 200 million yen ($1.61 million).
A global fund for oil-related damages, to which Japan belongs, would then be used to help cover the difference.
Japanese companies, mostly oil companies, could be called on to jointly provide a maximum of about six billion yen ($48 million) to 6.5 billion yen ($52.4 million) as their share of the bill.

Analysts said the payment -- if it had to be made -- would be an unwelcome expenditure for Japanese oil companies suffering from shrinking profit margins. But they said the payments should not pose much of a problem.

"I think it's quite possible that some companies, which were expecting finally to be able to report a profit, would remain in the red," said Osuke Tazaki, an analyst with think tank Okasan Economic Research Institute.
He said, however, that the news would hardly serve to knock down oil companies' stock prices.

Tazaki and other industry analysts said the rising cost of crude oil and the tumbling value of the yen -- which erodes the purchasing power of Japanese firms -- were more worrisome factors in terms of the firms' bottom line.
"I think that the rise in fuel costs is a (larger) factor," said Hisashi Gohno, an analyst with Wako Research Institute.
The analysts did not provide any specific earnings estimates for companies, given the volatility of crude prices and foreign exchange rates.
But they said the oil companies would probably be able to raise the money to pay any oil pollution damages without too much difficulty, through sales of assets if necessary.
Takashi Kawai, an analyst at Nikko Research Center, said there were other factors apart from crude oil prices and foreign exchange rates that could have a significant impact on oil company earnings.
He said kerosene sales this winter appeared to be below expectations and that this could hurt earnings.
The terms of the international agreement for oil pollution damages divides the burden of payment between the member countries according to the volume of each country's crude oil imports.
Japan's share is about 30 percent, most of which will be paid by oil companies, with a much smaller volume provided by electric power utilities.

The maximum payment arising out the international agreement -- the International Convention on the Establishment of an International Fund for Compensation for Oil Pollution Damage -- would be about 22 billion yen ($177 million), industry sources said.

According to 1995 import figures, leading refiner Nippon Oil Co Ltd's maximum payment would be roughly 1 billion yen ($8.0 million), a company spokesman said. Most analysts said Nippon Oil could make the payment without much difficulty. ($1=124 yen)
